A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PLANETALIGN library and benchmark. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated results.

before.justification: v1 reports original effectiveness, scalability, robustness, supervision-sensitivity, and implementation-comparison experiments in Section 5 and Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and adds knowledge-graph diagnostic curves and large-graph runtime and out-of-memory results.

M1.justification: The library pipeline and fourteen alignment methods remain substantively unchanged in Section 4 and Appendix B. The Data-to-BaseData rename, optional-logger clarification, and documentation of returned embeddings and alignment matrices do not establish an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: The eighteen built-in datasets remain unchanged, but Figures 5–6 extend noise and supervision diagnostics from five domains to include knowledge graphs. The attributed DBP15K block is also relabeled from ZH–EN to FR–EN; the largely identical entries leave unclear whether this corrects a label or changes the evaluated language pair.

E2.justification: The fourteen benchmark methods and ten methods in the retained official-implementation comparison are unchanged. The new large-graph experiment uses nine existing methods; it introduces no new comparator and does not replace the original comparison.

E3.justification: Appendix C changes the reported hyperparameter policy from official defaults to tuning five candidates per key parameter. This is a substantive protocol revision, although rerunning the retained results is not established. New Appendix D.4 tests training runtime on 50K, 75K, and 100K-node ER graphs with average degree 5, supplementing the retained degree-10 inference-scalability experiment.

E4.justification: Figures 5–6 add knowledge-graph results to the existing edge-noise, attribute-noise, supervision-noise, and training-ratio analyses. The diagnostic questions and the original five-domain analyses are otherwise substantially retained.

E5.justification: Both versions describe five randomly seeded splits and five runs per split, with means and standard deviations. Detailed uncertainty entries remain in the relocated result tables. The new domain summaries do not replace those entries, and no new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Table 6 adds substantial large-graph runtime and memory-failure evidence, and Figures 5–6 add knowledge-graph curves. Most detailed benchmark values are retained. In the relabeled attributed DBP15K block, PARROT's Hits@1/Hits@10/MRR change from 0.7733/0.9361/0.8316 to 0.8737/0.9550/0.9040; the ZH–EN-to-FR–EN label change prevents interpreting this as a same-setting gain. The official-comparison table also changes SLOTAlign's PLANETALIGN MRR from 0.1991 to 0.200, beyond equivalent rounding.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 changes the stated N in Hits@K and MRR from the number of testing nodes to the number of nodes, dropping the explicit restriction on the averaging population. The equations otherwise remain identical, and an actual evaluation change is not established. The added OT discussion is conceptual and introduces no theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a library containing eighteen datasets and fourteen methods, with comparable implementation accuracy and up to threefold speedup. The introduction additionally claims theoretical insights, supported by a new qualitative explanation of OT's advantages in Section 5.2.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 adds explanations involving global constrained optimization, marginal constraints, and transport costs. Appendix D.4 adds an interpretation of intrinsic scalability limits, while Section 7 develops specific plans for dynamic, simultaneous multi-network, and cross-domain alignment and more efficient computation. Most existing empirical interpretations and takeaways remain unchanged.

D1.justification: New Table 4 specifies key-parameter search spaces across all fourteen methods, substantially expanding the previous referral to official defaults. Section 4.2 also documents returned intermediate outputs and clarifies API usage. Hardware, split/run counts, and the principal code and documentation links remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands application citations and connections to other research. Its roadmap introduces concrete links to work such as GOT, MrMine, dynamic network alignment, active alignment, and low-rank or sliced optimal transport. The positioning against the same five existing alignment libraries remains intact.

P1.justification: Most section order and narrative remain recognizable. v2 condenses related work, revises API explanations, adds a robustness summary, separates limitations into Section 7, and adds an appendix contents page. Conference statements replace the NeurIPS checklist, with the LLM declaration retained separately.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, and Figure 4 separates the original scalability display into six panels grouped by method family. Table 2 becomes a domain-level summary, with original dataset results merged and relocated to the appendix. Figures 5–6 expand to six domains, and new hyperparameter and large-graph tables plus Figure 7 substantially revise the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: Explicit search spaces, clearer domain summaries and scalability displays, and additional large-graph evidence modestly improve the paper's documentation and practical usefulness. The gains are limited by unresolved protocol and dataset-label changes and a new numerical inconsistency: Table 6 reports JOENA's 50K runtimes as 2,310 versus 22,800 seconds while claiming a 1.01x speedup. These issues limit confidence in the added evidence, despite the presentation benefits.
